topic: kubectl commands every DevOps engineer must know
linkedin_hook: Mastering kubectl is no longer a choice, it's a necessity for every DevOps engineer working with Kubernetes
linkedin_intro: As a seasoned DevOps engineer, I've compiled a list of essential kubectl commands that I use daily to manage and troubleshoot my Kubernetes clusters. In this cheatsheet, I'll share the most critical commands that every DevOps engineer should know. From basic commands to advanced troubleshooting, this cheatsheet has got you covered.

items.description: Lists all pods in the current namespace
Lists all deployments in the current namespace
Lists all services in the current namespace
Lists all nodes in the cluster
Displays information about the cluster
Creates a new pod named my-pod with the nginx image
Deletes the pod named my-pod
Displays detailed information about the pod named my-pod
Displays the logs of the pod named my-pod
Executes a command in the pod named my-pod and opens a new shell session
Creates a new deployment named my-deployment with the nginx image
Displays the rollout status of the deployment named my-deployment
Displays the rollout history of the deployment named my-deployment
Undoes the last rollout of the deployment named my-deployment
Scales the deployment named my-deployment to 3 replicas
Creates a new clusterip service named my-service that exposes port 80
Lists all services in the current namespace
Displays detailed information about the service named my-service
Deletes the service named my-service
Exposes the deployment named my-deployment as a load balancer service on port 80
Lists all events in the current namespace
Displays detailed information about the node named my-node
Displays the resource usage of the pod named my-pod
Displays the resource usage of the node named my-node
Creates a new pod for debugging purposes with the ubuntu image

pro_tips: Use kubectl with the --v=5 flag to increase the verbosity of the output and get more detailed information about the commands being executed
Use kubectl config use-context to switch between different Kubernetes contexts and clusters
Use kubectl apply -f to apply configuration files to your cluster, and kubectl diff -f to see the differences between the current state and the desired state
Use kubectl rollout restart to restart all pods in a deployment, and kubectl rollout pause to pause a deployment
